criteria.reason: Both plans stay focused on one coherent lesson about the Roman Empire's extent and Mediterranean connectivity, with well-formed verb-first Portuguese skills, concrete examples, and real-life uses.

A progresses cleanly from Italy to the three Mediterranean shores and beyond to Britain and Mesopotamia, testing transfer with new ports and cities, while B's checks repeat the exact Egyptian grain and Britain examples already taught.

A pairs every geographic screen and question with an appropriate map and valid mapExplorer coordinates, whereas B puts northern Britain at latitude 58.44 outside the roman-empire-117 map's 23-to-57 range in two activities and leaves its guess and sea-route screens without visuals.
Both fit the beginner level and lesson scope well, but B uses Brazilian Portuguese quotation conventions throughout while A uses European Portuguese guillemets on screens 10 and 11.

observations.claim: Screens 6 and 8 use coordinates (58,44; -3,09) for northern Britain on the roman-empire-117 base map, which exceeds the base map's allowed latitude range of 23 to 57.
observations.learnerCost: The writer cannot place the northern Britain pin on the roman-empire-117 map as planned, breaking both the explanation explorer and the main map activity.

observations.claim: Screen 3 asks about traveling around the entire Mediterranean coastline before any map has been shown, and screen 5 explains the maritime supply route from Egypt to Rome with visual set to null.
observations.learnerCost: A beginner has to picture the Mediterranean coastline and the Egypt-to-Rome sea route in their head instead of seeing them on a map.

observations.claim: Screen 8 asks the learner to locate named regions with labels hidden until tapped, which does not match how mapExplorer works (tapping pins to uncover clues for a check question).
observations.learnerCost: The writer receives an interaction brief that conflicts with the chosen map template and will have to redesign the activity.

location.detail: pedir que o aluno localize Hispânia (40,42; -3,70), Gália (45,76; 4,84) e Egito (31,20; 29,92), com os nomes ocultos até cada escolha.

observations.claim: Screen 7's check reuses the exact Egypt-to-Rome wheat example already stated in screens 1 and 5 as a leading two-option recall question, and screen 8's check repeats the exact southern-versus-northern Britain comparison from screen 6.
observations.learnerCost: The learner is tested on memorizing the lesson's own examples rather than applying the geographic ideas to new places.

observations.claim: Screen 6 justifies Tarraco and Éfeso as a distractor for confusing distance with changing shores, even though Tarraco (Europe) and Éfeso (Asia) actually are on different shores of the Mediterranean, just not Europe and Africa.
observations.learnerCost: The writer may write misleading distractor feedback claiming Tarraco and Éfeso share the same shore.

location.detail: use Tarraco e Éfeso como distração para quem confunde distância com mudança de margem.

observations.claim: Screens 10 and 11 use European Portuguese guillemets («nenhuma» and «Em 117 d.C., ...») instead of standard Brazilian Portuguese quotation marks.
observations.learnerCost: The punctuation looks slightly foreign to a Brazilian reader unless the writer normalizes it.

location.detail: ofereça «nenhuma» para quem supõe que Roma governava toda a ilha.

overall.reason: A gives the writer an accurate, visually complete plan with valid map coordinates and strong transfer checks, whereas B breaks the roman-empire-117 map bounds in two activities and relies on repetitive recall checks.

criteria.reason: A and B have the exact same well-scoped single skill, canonical topic, concrete example, and real-life use case.
B gets the screen 5 check right (making fewer t-shirts lowers total fabric cost), while A reverses the answer key and falsely claims total fabric cost stays the same.
Both plans are identical on visuals and activities, appropriately staying text-only where nothing needs to be pictured and using categorize for sorting fixed and variable costs.
Both plans use identical, natural beginner-level Brazilian Portuguese and stay tightly within the lesson scope.

observations.claim: Screen 5 asks what happens to the total cost of fabric when a workshop makes fewer t-shirts at the same fabric price and gives the wrong answer key (ficar igual) while marking the true answer (diminuir) as the tempting wrong choice.
observations.learnerCost: The writer would create a check that marks the right answer wrong and teaches the exact opposite of how variable costs behave, contradicting the rest of the lesson.

location.detail: Resposta: ficar igual, porque o preço do tecido não muda; incluir “diminuir” como a resposta tentadora.

overall.reason: A and B are identical except for screen 5, where A has a major answer-key error that contradicts the definition of a variable cost and B gets it right.
